idiom_name: single state-reference rebinding (plus java.util.Collections.swap for lists)
implementation_notes: Java has no user-defined assignment, no swap protocol and no noexcept; what replaces the classic structure is reference semantics. Keep the representation behind one reference field and install a new state by rebinding it - a plain assignment that neither allocates nor can fail, so a rollback path that assigns the previous reference back is trivially safe. For lists, java.util.Collections.swap(list, i, j) is the standard-library exchange (O(1) for RandomAccess lists, but it throws IndexOutOfBoundsException and only works on mutable lists), and for state shared between threads java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference (getAndSet/compareAndSet/compareAndExchange) or a VarHandle gives an atomic exchange of one reference. A multi-field exchange cannot be made atomic, so everything that must be published together belongs in a single immutable holder.
pitfalls: Collections.swap throws IndexOutOfBoundsException (and UnsupportedOperationException on immutable lists), so it is not an infallible exchange unless you bounds-check first - a rollback path cannot treat it as non-throwing.
A single reference write is atomic but two writes are not: swapping two references is not atomic, and two AtomicReferences cannot be exchanged as a pair - use one immutable holder and swap it.
final fields cannot be reassigned after construction and records expose final components; when the state is genuinely immutable, publish a new instance instead of swapping fields.
Every reference may be null: a swap can silently install a null state, so validate the fresh state before exchanging it.
